canonical_definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats generalization as a model, method, or agent's capacity to maintain useful performance on unseen data, tasks, domains, or conditions, often under distribution shift and often contrasted with memorization or overfitting; one recurring formulation asks whether results reflect "genuine ability or just memorization of the training data." Many papers make this concrete as transfer to new instructions, tools, languages, modalities, environments, users, or harder problems without task-specific retraining. A smaller line uses the same term more narrowly for held-out test performance from the same distribution, for logically or semantically transformed inputs such as reversed relations or rephrased prompts, or for specialized settings like knowledge editing, abstention, attacks, and merged models.

Space of facets. Papers use several near-synonyms for the broad transfer notion, including generalizability, generalization ability, generalization capability, generalization performance, and British-spelling variants. They also carve out narrower subtypes such as task-agnostic generalizability, domain-generality, single-task generalization, and sequence generalization. The main contrasts are with memorization, overfitting, shortcut learning, and specialization; in editing work, generalization is also discussed alongside locality and reliability, and in abstention work alongside specificity. A smaller set of papers reserves generality for preserving the union of skills in merged models or for making an edit apply across related inputs.

Space of measurement. Operationalization is broad: papers link generalization to 141 measurement instruments and 23 behavioral indicators. The most frequent instruments are MMLU, MT-Bench, ARC-Challenge, GSM8K, and GPQA, and most operationalizations use benchmark performance on unseen tasks, out-of-domain datasets, cross-domain transfers, or seen versus unseen splits. Many papers also use embodied, multimodal, tool-use, retrieval, web, and editing benchmarks, while smaller lines use human evaluation, GPT-4 or other LLM-as-a-judge comparisons, or analytical quantities such as generalization error and bounds. These measurements usually match the dominant definition of transfer beyond training, but some narrower operationalizations target rephrased or neighboring edit queries, abstention on descendant concepts, or ordinary held-out test sets rather than broader distribution shifts.

Links. Across linked constructs, papers most often connect generalization to in-context learning, memorization, reasoning, robustness, and overfitting, with many other constructs also appearing. Papers claim causal relationships in both directions between generalization and in-context learning, while memorization is treated as related to generalization, reported to correlate with it in one training study, and also linked by causal claims that memorization can lead to limited or poor generalization. Reasoning is both related to generalization and claimed to causally support it; robustness is both related to it and linked by causal claims in both directions; overfitting is related to generalization, and papers claim causal relationships from overfitting to reduced generalization. A smaller group of papers also reports correlations with additional constructs and relatedness links outside these five.

characterization_sections.label: Space of definitions.
characterization_sections.text: Across papers, the prevailing usage treats generalization as a model, method, or agent's capacity to maintain useful performance on unseen data, tasks, domains, or conditions, often under distribution shift and often contrasted with memorization or overfitting; one recurring formulation asks whether results reflect "genuine ability or just memorization of the training data." Many papers make this concrete as transfer to new instructions, tools, languages, modalities, environments, users, or harder problems without task-specific retraining. A smaller line uses the same term more narrowly for held-out test performance from the same distribution, for logically or semantically transformed inputs such as reversed relations or rephrased prompts, or for specialized settings like knowledge editing, abstention, attacks, and merged models.

characterization_sections.label: Space of facets.
characterization_sections.text: Papers use several near-synonyms for the broad transfer notion, including generalizability, generalization ability, generalization capability, generalization performance, and British-spelling variants. They also carve out narrower subtypes such as task-agnostic generalizability, domain-generality, single-task generalization, and sequence generalization. The main contrasts are with memorization, overfitting, shortcut learning, and specialization; in editing work, generalization is also discussed alongside locality and reliability, and in abstention work alongside specificity. A smaller set of papers reserves generality for preserving the union of skills in merged models or for making an edit apply across related inputs.

characterization_sections.label: Space of measurement.
characterization_sections.text: Operationalization is broad: papers link generalization to 141 measurement instruments and 23 behavioral indicators. The most frequent instruments are MMLU, MT-Bench, ARC-Challenge, GSM8K, and GPQA, and most operationalizations use benchmark performance on unseen tasks, out-of-domain datasets, cross-domain transfers, or seen versus unseen splits. Many papers also use embodied, multimodal, tool-use, retrieval, web, and editing benchmarks, while smaller lines use human evaluation, GPT-4 or other LLM-as-a-judge comparisons, or analytical quantities such as generalization error and bounds. These measurements usually match the dominant definition of transfer beyond training, but some narrower operationalizations target rephrased or neighboring edit queries, abstention on descendant concepts, or ordinary held-out test sets rather than broader distribution shifts.

characterization_sections.label: Links.
characterization_sections.text: Across linked constructs, papers most often connect generalization to in-context learning, memorization, reasoning, robustness, and overfitting, with many other constructs also appearing. Papers claim causal relationships in both directions between generalization and in-context learning, while memorization is treated as related to generalization, reported to correlate with it in one training study, and also linked by causal claims that memorization can lead to limited or poor generalization. Reasoning is both related to generalization and claimed to causally support it; robustness is both related to it and linked by causal claims in both directions; overfitting is related to generalization, and papers claim causal relationships from overfitting to reduced generalization. A smaller group of papers also reports correlations with additional constructs and relatedness links outside these five.

A few papers apply the term to prompts, attacks, edits, or other components, but they still use the same core idea of effectiveness extending to novel cases rather than a different phenomenon.
